newsitem.title: USA: For-profit hospitals have higher costs - study.
newsitem.headline: For-profit hospitals have higher costs - study.

text.p: For-profit hospitals spend at least 23 percent more on administrative costs and rack up higher overall bills than public or not-for-profit hospitals, according to a new study.

The finding by Drs. Steffie Woolhandler and David Himmelstein of Harvard Medical School in Thursday's New England Journal of Medicine comes at a time of continued concern about the high cost of health care in general and the amount of money spent to administer hospitals in particular.

Nearly 25 cents of every dollar spent by hospitals in the United States goes to administration, nearly twice the rate in Canada. Although for-profit hospitals claim to be more efficient than others, research done up to the 1980s found they tend to cost more and have higher administrative outlays.

The new study was designed to see if those conclusions remained valid. Using 1994 Medicare data from 6,227 hospitals, it found that at for-profit hospitals 34 cents of each dollar was spent on administration, compared to 25 cents for private not-for-profit hospitals and 23 cents for public institutions.

They also found that between 1990 and 1994 the increase in spending for administration was greatest among for-profit hospitals. Those higher administrative costs were a major reason why the overall cost of treating an average patient was $8,115 at for-profit hospitals versus $7,490 at not-for-profit hospitals and $6,507 at public hospitals.

"We found that for-profit hospitals spend 23 percent more on administration than do comparable private not-for-profit hospitals and 34 percent more than public institutions," the researchers concluded.

They also looked at how quickly administrative costs rose in hospitals that switched between for-profit and not-for-profit status. Of the 75 that became for-profit facilities, administrative costs rose 2.5 percentage points. Among the 105 for-profit hospitals that became not-for-profit or public facilities between 1990 and 1994, the costs for administration rose only 0.4 percentage points.
Woolhandler and Himmelstein said administration costs may keep growing because "success increasingly requires business acumen, coordination and control of the clinical workforce."
"Contrary to the rhetoric of the market, market forces are apparently 'upsizing' administration," they said.
